questions.prompt: Tell me about yourself and your background in instructional design.
questions.answer: I started as a high-school history and English teacher and moved into corporate instructional design and enterprise enablement. My current work centers on learning for sellers and partners working with complex technical products. I build product-launch learning, microlearning, interactive practice, certification paths, and live workshops. I also work hands-on with LMS administration, AI evaluation, reporting automation, and multimedia production when those pieces are part of the learning problem.

questions.prompt: Walk me through an instructional design project you owned end to end.
questions.answer: My Enterprise Sales Certification Pathway is the clearest end-to-end example. I took product, technical, and sales source material; defined seller-focused objectives; organized the material into a multi-course path; built lessons, scenarios, knowledge checks, and assessment content in Rise and Storyline; coordinated SME review and QA; tested learner paths in the LMS; and supported reporting and maintenance after release. The scope extended beyond course authoring because the certification also had routing, regional requirements, LMS behavior, and reporting needs.

questions.prompt: How do you design technical training for a non-technical or sales audience?
questions.answer: I do not try to turn sellers into engineers. I work backward from the decisions the audience actually has to make: recognize fit, ask useful discovery questions, explain value, compare solution paths, choose a next step, or know when specialist support is needed. Technical detail stays when it supports one of those decisions. That keeps the learning accurate without letting product or engineering source material take over the course.

questions.prompt: How do you work with subject matter experts and reviewers?
questions.answer: I try to make SME review specific instead of asking someone to react to an entire course at once. I start from approved source material, identify what decision or objective each section supports, and use review cycles to verify accuracy, positioning, assessment logic, and anything that changed in the source. I keep instructional decisions separate from factual approval so SMEs can focus on the content they own while I keep responsibility for the learning experience, structure, and usability.

questions.prompt: How do you design for learners with different levels of experience?
questions.answer: I separate what everyone needs from what only some learners need. In certification work, that has meant keeping shared seller decisions in the core path, separating regional requirements, and moving deeper technical foundations into optional learning when they are not necessary for every seller. I also use expandable detail, comparisons, quick references, and scenarios so experienced learners can move efficiently without leaving newer learners without context.

questions.prompt: How do you approach assessment design?
questions.answer: I start with the decision or behavior the learner should demonstrate, then choose the lightest assessment that can show it. For sales learning, I prefer practice that asks the learner to identify opportunity fit, compare solution paths, interpret customer information, or choose a next step rather than only recall product facts. I use formative checks throughout the learning and reserve final assessment for the evidence that matters to completion or certification.

questions.prompt: What is your approach to scenario-based or interactive learning?
questions.answer: I use interaction when the learner needs to make a decision, not just because a page needs more clicks. I build scenarios around realistic evidence, customer conversations, qualification choices, or positioning decisions, then use feedback to explain the reasoning behind the stronger choice. I also build browser-based interaction demos when HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are a better fit for the experience I want to prototype.

questions.prompt: What did you do during the Absorb to Docebo migration?
questions.answer: My migration work covered the content and learner-experience layer of the move from Absorb to Docebo. questions.prompt: How do you measure learning or work with reporting?
questions.answer: I work with the evidence that the system and project can actually support. That includes completion and certificate data, assessment results, learner-path exceptions, support patterns, and operational reporting. When LMS reporting has not matched the learning design, I have built supplemental workflows instead of pretending the limitation did not exist. One example uses four recurring LMS reports and Python-based analysis to produce Complete and Incomplete review sheets with learner type and visible exceptions.

questions.prompt: What experience do you have evaluating or training AI systems?
questions.answer: My AI work focuses on evaluating model outputs against the task, approved evidence, scoring criteria, and the needs of the intended user. I look for instruction-following failures, unsupported claims, logic gaps, writing-quality problems, and subtle issues that make an answer less useful even when it sounds polished. I also write actionable feedback and use rubrics and calibration to keep judgments consistent.

questions.prompt: How do you decide when learner-facing AI belongs in a learning experience?
questions.answer: I would use learner-facing AI when the experience needs to respond to a learner's role, choices, or reasoning, rather than repeat a fixed lesson. I start with the task, define what the system may use, and check whether its feedback helps the learner make a better decision. The Learner-facing AI page illustrates five possible patterns with fictional content. My Hiring Guide is a live, contained example of question routing and evidence linking; it uses reviewed answers rather than a generative model. Those examples show my design approach, not a claim that every pattern shipped in a client program.

questions.prompt: How do you handle fast-changing product content or shifting source material?
questions.answer: I design for maintenance from the beginning when I know the product or source material will keep changing. I keep modules and interactions as independent as practical, track which source owns a claim or section, avoid publishing information that is not approved yet, and isolate regional or optional content when it will change on a different schedule. That makes future updates smaller and reduces the chance that one change forces a complete rebuild.

questions.prompt: How do you describe your role when a project was completed by a larger team?
questions.answer: I separate what I personally owned from what the larger team or program owned. For example, I can say that I facilitated assigned MEDDPICC modules without claiming ownership of the entire workshop curriculum, or that I handled LMS content administration, UAT, support, and learner-experience work without claiming that I architected the entire platform migration. I would rather be precise about my contribution than make a project sound larger by blurring ownership.

questions.prompt: How do you talk about results when confidential metrics or direct ROI are not available?
questions.answer: I do not manufacture ROI or imply that a metric exists when I cannot support it publicly. I use the evidence I actually have: what was delivered, how the learner path changed, what decisions the design supported, what QA or reporting problem was solved, and what operational workflow was created. When confidential or unapproved metrics are not available, I say that clearly and use public-safe recreated examples to show the quality of the work instead.
